results.title: Products & Environmental Services - Southern Group of State Foresters
results.content: ## Southern forests produce over $100 billion in forest products and markets around the world. Working forests support the southern economy and are responsible for the production of renewable products like lumber, paper products, bioenergy and thousands of other everyday items. Forests also provide ecosystem services like air and water filtration, oxygen production and carbon sequestration, while providing open natural spaces for countless outdoor recreation opportunities. ### Growing the Future: Celebrating the Impact of Southern Forest Products. Forestry and the forest products industry contributes more than $251 billion to the South’s economy. U.S. southern forests, forestry and the forest products industry provides for:. ## Forest Products and Markets. While timber and its many by-products are the primary resource generated by well-managed, sustainable working forests, each southern state has its own unique mix of wood resources, services, manufacturing innovations and investment opportunities. Primary forest products companies produce lumber, plywood, pulp, paper and other wood products using roundwood logs as a raw material. Secondary forest product companies produce furniture, wood fixtures, molding, trusses and other engineered wood commodities, using products from primary mills as inputs. Trees also provide non-timber products including pine straw, firewood, food, medicines and other non-timber and specialty forest products. In addition, the use of renewable, sustainable forest biomass for bio-based products may help decrease the risk of wildfires through the removal of brush, small diameter trees, damaged trees and other fuel sources which could otherwise worsen future wildfire activity if left in the forest. Forests provide significant environmental benefits including protecting air and water quality, capturing and filtering storm water, storing carbon, enhancing wildlife habitat, supplying renewable energy, reducing energy consumption and delivering quality of life benefits. Promoting the use of forest products as a substitute for carbon-intensive alternatives like concrete and steel not only helps increase carbon storage but also supports forest retention. Southern forests are productive, dynamic, and diverse, supporting a vast array of wildlife communities. ### Primary Forest Products Locator. Use the Primary Forest Products Locator to locate mills and companies which produce lumber, plywood, pulp, paper and other wood products. results.title: What Drives Employment in Forestry and Wood Processing? | Global Forests
results.content: # What Drives Employment in Forestry and Wood Processing? One has to ask whether this is the start of a new downward spiral in wood harvesting and employment in the United States, similar to what happened from the late 1990s to 2010 (Figure 1), or whether it is a temporary blip. Figure 2 presents total harvests and the inventory of harvestable tree volume in the United States since the early part of the last century. As a a result, employment in wood products, including pulp and paper, fell from more than 1 million people in 1914 to 890,000 in 1921 (US Census of Manufacturers, 1930). Employment in wood processing fell in regions most heavily affected by these forest set-asides – including Oregon, Washington, California, and other western states. Employment in wood processing, and especially pulp processing, fell. No doubt, access to trees affects employment – just witness what happened in the eastern US at the beginning of the twentieth century and the Pacific Northwestern US at the end of it – but tree supply is not a problem today. Despite a surfeit of trees, and falling wood prices (Figure 4), wood processing mills are closing all over the US these days, including the South. It turns out that access to trees isn’t everything in the wood processing sector. For a long time, this competitive advantage translated into strong growth in the wood products sector, especially in the US South, but also in other regions. Unlike last century, when limitations in the supply of trees created bottlenecks, today the primary factors affecting employment in wood processing have largely to do with pressures external to the forestry sector. Deeper investments in pellet-based boilers and the emerging mass-timber sector could reverse this price trend (see Favero et al., 2023; Lan et al., 2025), but investments in capacity for mass timber and wood-based biomass energy have not been strong enough to date to switch the current price trend. So what does this mean for a  place like Chillicothe, Ohio, which hung onto its pulp mill for over 200 years even as America’s wood basket moved south and west in the 1900s?
